title: Sternal Dehiscence After Figure-of-Eight Wire Closure in High-Risk Cardiac Surgery: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study
content:
Background: Figure-of-eight wire closure is a commonly used method of sternal approximation after cardiac surgery. Its postoperative complication profile in patients with impaired wound-healing characteristics merits detailed description, particularly with respect to the clinical course of dehiscence and subsequent revision.
Methods: We retrospectively evaluated 72 consecutive high-risk adults among 245 patients undergoing cardiac surgery between February 4, 2025, and February 12, 2026, at a single institution. High risk was defined as obesity, diabetes mellitus, and/or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. All included patients underwent full median sternotomy followed by primary figure-of-eight closure. The primary outcome was new sternal dehiscence within 90 postoperative days, assessed clinically and by thoracic computed tomography in affected patients. Associations were examined using exploratory univariable tests; an operative subgroup analysis compared coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)-containing and valve-only procedures.
Results: Ten of 72 patients developed sternal dehiscence (13.9%; 95% Wilson confidence interval, 7.7%–23.7%); three cases were diagnosed within 30 days and seven between days 31 and 90. Superficial culture-positive wound infection was documented in 15 patients (20.8%), including all ten with dehiscence. All ten affected patients underwent revision with bilateral Robicsek reinforcement and figure-of-eight wiring within 48–72 hours of diagnosis. At four months after the index operation, two patients showed complete osseous union on computed tomography and eight had stable approximation without complete fusion; no recurrent dehiscence was documented. Dehiscence was observed in 9/53 CABG-containing procedures (17.0%) and 1/19 valve-only procedures (5.3%).
Conclusions: In this selected high-risk single-arm cohort, the 90-day observed incidence of sternal dehiscence was 13.9%. The series documents mechanical findings, associated superficial infection, and short-term findings after surgical revision. Its design does not support comparative conclusions about closure efficacy or the independent causation of dehiscence.
